title: Matsya, the fish in Manu's hands
word: the ten avatars as a series
hook: a fingertip fish asks a praying king to keep it safe
carry: the lord can come as the smallest creature
tomorrow: the fish says a flood is coming. what goes in the boat?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten avatars as a series: many shapes, one refrain, and a fish at the head of the row. Today, why a fish the size of a fingertip asks a king for help.

What if the Lord of everything came small enough to fit in your hands? Early morning, at the water: a king named Manu is cupping water in his hands to offer it, and there's something in his palms. A fish, no bigger than a fingertip. It speaks. Please, it says, keep me safe. In the water, the big fish eat the small ones. That's the whole reason, and it's enough for Manu.
screen: `SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD.` → `A FISH IN MANU'S PALMS.` → `KEEP ME SAFE.`

segments.voice: That's how the Matsya Purana opens the story, and the Bhagavata Purana tells it too, where the king is called Satyavrata. Manu was in the middle of a prayer, offering water, the way many Hindus still pour water as an offering each morning. He doesn't toss the fish back. He takes it home and puts it in a water jar. By the next day it has outgrown the jar. He moves it to a pool, and it fills that. A lake, then a river, and each time the fish grows to fill the space it's given. At last he brings it to the ocean, and it fills even that. Only then does Manu ask who it is. It is Vishnu, the first descent in the row. Here's the teaching inside it. This is what Hindus mean by an avatar: God coming down into a shape we can meet. Vishnu's name is often explained as the one who pervades everything; no jar can hold him. Yet he comes first as the smallest thing there is, asking for help. In the Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase, that the Lord lives in the heart of every being. So a creature in your hands is never just a creature. It's one reason many Hindu families set out food for birds or cows before they eat. And notice: Manu cared for the fish before he knew who it was. Then, in the ocean, the fish tells him why it came: a flood is on its way.
screen: `A FISH IN A WATER JAR.` · `JAR, POOL, LAKE, RIVER, SEA.` · `THE ONE WHO FILLS EVERYTHING, MADE SMALL.` · then, large: `THE LORD LIVES IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: If you have a cup of water, hold it in both hands, the way Manu held the river water, and pour a little, slowly, onto a plant or the ground outside, as many Hindus pour water as a morning offering. While it pours, bring to mind one small creature or person in your care. If you don't pray, simply water the plant and notice who depends on you.
The ten avatars as a series: Vishnu's descents in a row, and Matsya, the fish, comes first.
screen: `THE TEN AVATARS AS A SERIES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Something to keep: the Lord can come as the smallest creature, asking to be kept safe. Day done.

howItsDone: Matsya's story is retold from the Matsya and Bhagavata Puranas in homes and temple talks, and he is pictured as the first of Vishnu's descents, often as a fish below and Vishnu above. Many Hindus offer water each morning, and many families set out food for birds or animals before a meal.

fork.setup: an ant is crossing the kitchen counter. your little cousin goes to squash it, and Nani scoops it onto a leaf and carries it outside. 'why??' by Matsya's story?

fork.reveal: Manu kept a fingertip fish safe before he knew it was Vishnu. Hindu teaching says the Lord lives in the heart of every being, so even an ant is worth carrying outside.

original.note: Sanskrit matsya: fish. The name of Vishnu's first descent, and of the Purana that tells it.
